title: Fast Feedback is Effective Feedback: Here’s How to Do Better
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart contends that students improve through feedback rather than grades, and that feedback must be fast to be useful, using a coach who debriefs a game a week late as the analogy. Given three options, slow feedback, sacrificed evenings or smarter and pickier feedback, he chooses the third and shows what that looks like for pop-up debates, articles of the week and essays. Debates get in-the-moment interruptions and written reflection with no rubric, articles of the week are graded for knowledge-building without individual comment, and essays come back the next class via whole-class hit-list lessons, shorthand coding or a short taught rubric. He never covers papers in comments and times his grading like an athlete. He cites his ninth-graders' AP World History results as evidence the approach works, and concludes that clarity of purpose saves time and sanity.
points: Feedback, not grades, is what makes students better, and delayed feedback loses its value because learners no longer remember the performance.
Clarity about an assignment's purpose can eliminate individual feedback altogether, as with knowledge-building articles of the week.
Essay feedback can be next-day through hit-list lessons, shorthand codes based on class-built lists, or a simple rubric of up to seven explicitly taught skills.
Timing grading with a stopwatch and refusing to cover papers in comments trades volume of commentary for speed and impact.
quotes: It's not grades that make a student become a better writer or speaker or knowledge-builder — it's feedback.
The thing is, feedback generally needs to be fast if it's going to be useful, meaningful, or an effective use of the teacher's time.

A token grade may go into the grade book, but no rubrics and very little in the way of individualized feedback. This isn't because those are bad things — it's because they're not necessary, and I don't have time to do unnecessary things.
So look: no feedback given, tons of time saved, all because I'm clear about the purpose of the AoW assignment. Clear thinking saves us time and sanity.

A whole class “hit list” lesson where I teach toward and give examples of a specific skill or deficiency I'm finding in multiple sample student papers. This method requires me to read 10 or so papers out of a 60 paper set.

Fast feedback is effective feedback, and so we've got to get smarter (and pickier) about how and when we give feedback. A next-day hit list lesson will get your students further — both skill-wise and motivationally — than a two-weeks-later paper covered in comments.
